newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - BoF backs stable franc, praises EU pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BoF backs stable franc, praises EU pact.

text.p: Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet reaffirmed his iron-clad commitment to a stable franc on Tuesday and praised a new European Union budget pact as a milestone on the road to a single currency.

Trichet, speaking at an annual policy-setting news conference, made clear there would be no change in the Bank's policy of targeting moderate money supply growth and currency stability in pursuit of its primary goal of price stability.

"We are inflexibly attached to the stability of the franc among the most solid currencies in Europe," Trichet said, adding that the franc's stability had allowed market and official interest rates to fall significantly in France.
In a move widely seen as a stamp of approval of the "stability pact" agreed at an EU summit in Dublin last Friday, the Bank of France trimmed two key interest rates just before Trichet spoke.
It shaved its intervention rate by five percentage points to 3.15 percent from 3.20 percent. It cut another less crucial one, the five-to-10 day rate, to 4.60 percent from 4.75 percent.

"This is a very good sign the Bank of France is sending us," JP Morgan economist David Naude said of the rate cut. "It's really telling us it's happy with the stability pact, which nobody doubted, but it shows they've resumed easing," he said.
The EU pact is meant to impose strict budgetary discipline on nations participating in a single currency from 1999 and imposes fines on countries running excessive deficits.

Trichet said he was impressed with the pact, which would help to ensure the right mix between national fiscal policies and monetary policy from an independent European Central Bank (ECB) in the single-currency zone.
He also gave cautious approval to the idea of a stability council of ministers overseeing European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

A French idea, the council would offset the power of unelected European central bankers, "technocrats" according to French officials, over the single currency and by extension national economic policy, President Jacques Chirac has said.
Trichet said there would have to be "a very intense cooperation" among governments of nations inside the single currency zone and such co-operation in no way threatened the independence of the ECB.
The idea of questioning the independence of the ECB, guaranteed by the Maastricht treaty, was "not in the minds of anyone whatsoever in Paris", he said.

He had been asked his views on comments on Saturday by President Jacques Chirac that countries in the euro zone should hold summits and ministerial meetings to coordinate economic policies after the launch of the single European currency and act as a counterbalance to the power of the central bank.

Trichet's categorical support for the franc-mark link was expected since any deviation from this well-trod path could serve as fodder for those who believe the franc is too strong for the economy's good.
Former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing last month called for a sharp depreciation of the franc against the dollar to stimulate growth.
Political leaders and two members of the Bank of France's monetary policy council supported the call, while Trichet and the government rejected it.
